chunks: He said: Abu Ja'far Muhammad ibn Ali ibn al-Husayn reported to me, he said: Muhammad ibn al-Hasan ibn al-Walid narrated to us, he said: Muhammad ibn al-Hasan al-Saffar narrated to us, from Ya'qub ibn Yazid, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from more than one source, from Abu Abdillah Ja'far ibn Muhammad (peace be upon them both) who said:

"Manly virtues are of two types: the virtue of the hometown and the virtue of travel. As for the virtue of the hometown, it is recitation of the Quran, attending the mosques, keeping the company of good people, and pondering over religious jurisprudence. And as for the virtue of travel, it is offering one's provisions generously, jesting without indulging in what displeases God, minimizing disagreement with your travel companions, and not reporting on them once you have parted their company."

key_terms.الحضر: al-Hadar: being resident in one's hometown, settled life (opposite of travel)
key_terms.السفر: al-Safar: traveling, being on a journey away from home
key_terms.الفقه: al-Fiqh: Islamic jurisprudence, deep understanding of religious rulings
key_terms.المروءة: Muruwwa: manly virtue, chivalry, noble character encompassing both moral and social excellence

ai.seo_question: What are the two types of manly virtue (muruwwa) according to Imam Sadiq?
ai.summary: Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq (AS) defines two dimensions of muruwwa (manly virtue/chivalry), a concept central to pre-Islamic and Islamic Arab culture denoting noble character. At home, virtue is cultivated through spiritual and intellectual practices: Quran recitation, mosque attendance, associating with righteous people, and studying religious law. While traveling, virtue shifts to social generosity and consideration: sharing provisions, keeping cheerful company within God's limits, yielding to companions' preferences, and protecting their reputation after parting.
